power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "Standardized parameter estimates are shown; all coefficients were statistically significant (p < 0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

table.expanded: Fit improved further when a residual correlation between empathy and ego-resilience was included (χ² = 1.19, DF = 1, p = 0.276, CFI = 0.999, TLI = 0.994, RMSEA = 0.023 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.144], SRMR = 0.014).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.276", Sentence = "Fit improved further when a residual correlation between empathy and ego-resilience was included (χ² = 1.19, DF = 1, p = 0.276, CFI = 0.999, TLI = 0.994, RMSEA = 0.023 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.144], SRMR = 0.014)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Using the covariance matrix reported by Wang et al., we reexamined the evidence underlying their proposed mediation model relating empathy to lower perceived stress.
We show that the same pattern of associations can be accounted for by an alternative latent-variable model that does not assume the causal sequence proposed by the original authors.
In this alternative formulation, self-reported empathy, occupational commitment, ego-resilience, and perceived stress are treated as indicators of a broader latent trait, core self-evaluation.
The findings illustrate a general challenge in psychological research: a single covariance structure may be consistent with multiple theoretically plausible explanations.
As a result, correlational data alone rarely provide a sufficient basis for favoring one theoretical account over another.
We therefore argue that the evaluation of competing models should become a routine component of efforts to draw conclusions about psychological processes from observational data.
The study by Wang et al. Wang et al. (2026) analyzed responses from 359 nurses working in non-family-accompanied care wards in China, of whom 97.5% were women.

text.text: Participants completed measures assessing empathy, occupational commitment, ego-resilience, and perceived stress.

Based on a serial mediation model, the authors concluded that "empathy was negatively associated with perceived stress and was associated with perceived stress both directly and indirectly within the hypothesized serial mediation model through the sequential mediating pathway involving occupational commitment and ego-resilience" (p. 1).

On the basis of these findings, they further suggested that "interventions should move beyond isolated stress-reduction techniques and incorporate positive psychological resources, including empathic competence, occupational commitment, and egoresilience" (p. 12).
Although this interpretation is compatible with the observed data, it is not uniquely implied by them.
Correlational analyses generally do not permit definitive conclusions regarding causal ordering among psychological constructs (Reichenbach, 1971).
text.formatted: Correlational analyses generally do not permit definitive conclusions regarding causal ordering among psychological constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Reichenbach, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: Different causal structures can lead to the same covariance matrix, making it difficult to determine which explanation best reflects the underlying processes.
Consequently, conclusions about mechanisms may depend heavily on assumptions built into the statistical model rather than on the observed relationships themselves.
To demonstrate this issue, we present an alternative model that reproduces the reported associations while implying a substantially different theoretical interpretation.
All analyses were conducted in R 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2026) using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012).

text.text: Rather than specifying empathy as the starting point of a causal sequence culminating in reduced perceived stress, the model treats self-rated empathy, occupational commitment, ego-resilience, and perceived stress as observable indicators of a common latent factor, core self-evaluation.
Core self-evaluation refers to a person's overall . . . . .
2 assessment of their capabilities, value, and effectiveness (Judge et al., 2004; Extremera & Rey, 2018).

text.text: From this perspective, individuals with more favorable core self-evaluations would be expected to report greater empathy, stronger occupational commitment, higher ego-resilience, and lower perceived stress.

Fit improved further when a residual correlation between empathy and ego-resilience was included (χ² = 1.19, DF = 1, p = 0.276, CFI = 0.999, TLI = 0.994, RMSEA = 0.023 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.144], SRMR = 0.014).

As shown in Figure 1B, this residual association was negative, indicating an inverse relation between empathy and ego-resilience after accounting for their shared association with core self-evaluation.

text.text: The implications of this model differ markedly from those drawn by Wang et al.

Whereas the original article interpreted occupational commitment and ego-resilience as mechanisms through which empathy contributes to lower perceived stress, the latent-variable model views all four measured variables as reflections of the same underlying disposition.
Because both approaches can account for the reported covariance structure, the mediation pathway emphasized by Wang et al. cannot be considered the sole interpretation supported by the data.
Instead, the reported indirect effects may be at least partly a consequence of the way the model was specified rather than a uniquely determined feature of the observed relationships.
The present reanalysis demonstrates that the associations reported by Wang et al. can be interpreted within more than one coherent theoretical framework.

While the original study proposed a sequential process in which empathy reduces perceived stress through occupational commitment and ego-resilience, the alternative latent-variable model reproduces the same pattern of associations without assigning a causal priority to empathy.
The purpose of this commentary is not to claim that the model proposed by Wang et al. is necessarily incorrect.
Nor does the satisfactory performance of the alternative model establish that it represents the true underlying process.
Rather, the central point is that the available data are compatible with multiple explanations.
When competing models fit equally well, statistical fit indices alone cannot determine which theoretical account is more accurate.
This issue is especially important in the context of mediation analyses based on observational data.

Indirect effects are frequently interpreted as evidence for particular psychological mechanisms, yet cross-sectional and nonexperimental designs provide limited leverage for establishing causal direction.

When alternative models with divergent theoretical implications fit the same data, conclusions regarding mechanisms, intervention targets, and explanatory pathways necessarily depend on assumptions that remain untested.

Accordingly, findings from mediation analyses of observational datasets should generally be viewed as provisional interpretations rather than definitive evidence concerning underlying causal processes.
